en: NySBh_5,1.0: It was stated in brief that the multiplicity of *jātis* (futile rejoinders) arises from the various ways of opposing an argument through similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). This is now analyzed in detail. Indeed, when a probative reason (*sthāpanāhetu*) is employed, there are twenty-four types of refuting reasons (*pratiṣedhahetu*).

NyS_5,1.1: These are: similarity (*sādharmyasama*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*), parity by superiority (*utkarṣasama*), parity by inferiority (*apakarṣasama*), parity of the commendable (*varṇyasama*), parity of the non-commendable (*avarṇyasama*), parity of alternative (*vikalpasama*), parity of the provable (*sādhyasama*), parity of attainment (*prāptisama*), parity of non-attainment (*aprāptisama*), parity of consequence (*prasaṅgasama*), parity of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*), parity of non-arising (*anutpattisama*), parity of doubt (*saṃśayasama*), parity of the topic (*prakaraṇasama*), parity of the non-reason (*ahetusama*), parity of presumption (*arthāpattisama*), parity of non-distinction (*aviśeṣasama*), parity of demonstration (*upapattisama*), parity of perception (*upalabdhisama*), parity of non-perception (*anupalabdhisama*), parity of the eternal (*nityasama*), parity of the non-eternal (*anityasama*), and parity of the effect (*kāryasama*).
Since the genus (*jāti*) has been stated in brief, its detailed exposition must now be set forth; thus begins the Sūtra on Similarity and Dissimilarity (*sādharmya-ādi-sūtra*).

Similarity-based rejoinders (*sādharmya-sama*) and the others—namely, dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), augmentation (*utkarṣa*), diminution (*apakarṣa*), the praiseworthy (*varṇya*), the unpraiseworthy (*avarṇya*), alternative (*vikalpa*), the proven (*sādhya*), attainment (*prāpti*), non-attainment (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), non-arising (*anutpatti*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the topic (*prakaraṇa*), the non-reason (*ahetu*), implication (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), possibility (*upapatti*), perception (*upalabdhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), the eternal (*nitya*), the non-eternal (*anitya*), and the effect (*kārya*)—are all based on similarity. A similarity-based rejoinder (*sādharmya-sama*) is an objection raised through similarity that is not distinguished from the original probative reason (*sthāpanā-hetu*). It is defined as an opposition based on similarity.
We shall provide examples of that [non-distinction] here and there.
In this same manner, the fallacies beginning with *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the heterogeneity) are also to be explained.

When a conclusion is drawn through similarity or dissimilarity, the two fallacies known as "balancing the similarity" (sādharmya-sama) and "balancing the dissimilarity" (vaidharmya-sama) arise from the possibility of proving the opposite of that property.

NySBh_5.1.2: When a conclusion is drawn by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), the "balancing by similarity" (*sādharmyasama*) occurs when an opposition is raised by means of similarity itself, being no different from the original reason for the proposition (*sthāpanāhetu*), because the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is shown to be possible. For example: "The self possesses action (*kriyāvān*), because it is endowed with qualities that are causes of action in a substance; a clod of earth is a substance endowed with qualities that are causes of action and thus possesses action; likewise, the self is so; therefore, it possesses action."

When this has been presented, the opponent objects by means of similarity alone: "The self is inactive because it is an all-pervading substance, and space is all-pervading and inactive; likewise, the self is [all-pervading], therefore it is inactive.
And there exists no specific reason why, due to similarity with that which possesses action, it must be active, rather than, due to similarity with that which lacks action, it must be inactive.

Because there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other], the refutation based on similarity (*sādharmyasama*) occurs. Now, as for the refutation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*): a clod of earth is seen to be possessed of action due to its being endowed with the quality of being a cause of action and its being delimited; however, the self is not so. Therefore, it is argued that the self does not possess action like the clod of earth. Yet, there is no specific reason why, because of similarity to that which possesses action, it must necessarily possess action, rather than—because of dissimilarity to that which possesses action—it being devoid of action. Thus, due to the absence of a specific reason, this is a refutation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*).

And there is a conclusion by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇopasaṃhāra*): "The self is inactive because it is all-pervading; for a substance possessing action is seen to be non-pervasive, like a clod of earth, whereas the self is not like that; therefore, it is inactive. Objection by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa pratyavasthānam*): "A substance that is inactive is seen to be devoid of qualities that cause action, such as space (*ākāśa*); but the self is not like that; therefore, it is not inactive. Furthermore, there is no specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) to establish that because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action it must be inactive, rather than [the opposite] that because of its dissimilarity to that which lacks action it must possess action. Due to the absence of such a specific reason, this is the "balancing the dissimilar" (*vaidharmyasama*).

Now, [the fallacy of] "balancing the similar" (*sādharmyasama*) is as follows: A clod of earth is seen to possess action and to be endowed with qualities that are the causes of action; likewise, the self [is said to be so]. Therefore, it follows that the self possesses action. Yet, there is no specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) to establish that it is inactive because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action, rather than active because of its similarity to that which possesses action.
Due to the absence of such a specific reason, this is "balancing the similar."
Its establishment is like the establishment of a cow through the universal "cowness."

If the proof of the probandum were asserted merely through similarity or merely through dissimilarity, there would be a lack of definitive determination; however, that [proof] is not possible with respect to a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*). For instance, a cow is established as a cow by its "cowness," which is a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*), due to its similarity to other cows, and not by its connection with the dewlap and so forth.
A cow is established by the very nature of "cow-ness" (gotva) alone, due to its dissimilarity to horses and other animals, and not from a distinction of qualities and so forth.

This has already been explained in the section on the members [of a syllogism], where it was stated that "the performance of a single purpose through the mutual connection of the means of knowledge is common to a sentence.
Indeed, this lack of systematic order is based upon fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).

NS 5.1.4: Because of the variation in properties between the subject and the example, and because both may be unproven, there are the fallacies of *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *avarṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, and *sādhyasama*.
NySBh_5.1.4: *Utkarṣasama* (balancing the addition) occurs when one attributes a property of the example to the subject of the thesis (*sādhya*).

[For instance: "If the self possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action, like a clod of earth, then it follows that it must also possess touch, just like the clod of earth.
Or, if it does not possess touch like the clod of earth, then it cannot possess action either. Otherwise, a distinction [between the two cases] must be stated."

*Apakarṣasama* (balancing by subtraction) occurs when one attempts to apply the absence of the property in the probandum to the example. For instance: "A clod of earth is indeed seen to possess action and to be non-omnipresent; well then, let the self also possess action and be non-omnipresent, or else a distinction must be stated [between them]. *Varṇyasama* (balancing by the describable) and *avarṇyasama* (balancing by the non-describable) arise from reversing these two properties of the probandum and the example. *Varṇya* refers to that which is to be explained or described, while *avarṇya* is its opposite; these two constitute the balancing arguments based on the reversal of the properties of the subject and the example.

*Vikalpasama* (the equalizing by alternative) occurs when, based on an example endowed with the property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*), one introduces an alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) through an alternative regarding other properties.

For instance: "Just as some things endowed with the quality of being a cause of action are heavy, such as a clod of earth, while others are light, such as air; likewise, among those endowed with the quality of being a cause of action, some might possess action, like a clod of earth, while others might be devoid of action, like the self (*ātman*). Or rather, a distinction must be stated."

The property to be proven (*sādhya*) is that which possesses the power of the members [of a syllogism], such as the reason (*hetu*). One who applies that [property] to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) commits the fallacy of "equivalence to the probandum" (*sādhyasama*). If it follows that "as is the clod of earth, so is the self," then it also follows that "as is the self, so is the clod of earth. Now, this self is indeed to be proven as possessing action; therefore, the clod of earth must also be something to be proven. If this is not the case, then it is not true that "as is the clod of earth, so is the self."
The reply to these is:
"Because the application [of the reason] is established through some similarity, there is no refutation on account of dissimilarity. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.5)
The denial of what is established is inadmissible.

Furthermore, analogy is established because it possesses a commonality [with the object to be proven], as in the case: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. In that instance, it is not possible to raise an objection regarding a difference in properties between the cow and the gavaya.

Likewise, when a proving property (sādhaka-dharma) is endowed with the capacity of the example and other factors, it is not possible to state a refutation based on a difference in properties or a dissimilarity between the probandum (sādhya) and the example.
And because the example is established through the extension of the property to be proven.
In a case where there is agreement in cognition among ordinary people and experts, that non-erroneous object is extended [by analogy] for the purpose of making it known.
Thus, since the extension of the probandum (*sādhyātideśa*) is applicable to the example, it is untenable for the example itself to be the probandum.

NyS 5.1.7: Because a reason is indistinguishable whether it reaches the probandum or does not reach it—since it cannot establish [the probandum] if it does not reach it—the two [objections] based on reaching and non-reaching are [called] *prāptisama* and *aprāptisama*.

Does the reason (hetu) establish the probandum (sādhya) by reaching it or without reaching it? First of all, it does not establish it by reaching it; because there is no distinction in their state of having reached one another, it would not be an establishing factor. When two existing things have reached each other, which of them would be the establisher and which the established?
Without reaching the object to be accomplished, it does not exist; a lamp does not illuminate without having reached its object.
Opposition based on reaching is "balancing the reaching" (prāptisama); opposition based on non-reaching is "balancing the non-reaching" (aprāptisama).

The answer to these two is stated in Nyāyasūtra 5.1.8: "There is no prohibition [against the production of sound], because the production of jars and other things is observed, and because [sound] is produced by pressure and by sorcery."

In both ways, indeed, the negation is untenable: [on the one hand,] the agent, instrument, and locus produce the effect, such as a jar, from clay by reaching it; and [on the other hand,] in the case of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), when there is an act of affliction, it is observed that the means of accomplishment functions without reaching its object.

Because no reason is stated for the example, and because one counters with a counter-example, there are the two [fallacies] of "balancing the consequence" (prasaṅgasama) and "balancing the counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama).
The "balancing by consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) refutation is an objection raised on the grounds that, by implication, one must also state a proof for the proof itself.

For instance, when it is argued that "a clod of earth possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action," no further reason is provided; yet there can be no establishment [of a point] without a reason.
The "balancing by counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*) is an objection raised by means of a counter-example.

When it is argued that "the self possesses action because of its connection with qualities that are causes of action, like a clod of earth," a counter-example is offered: "space is seen to be devoid of action despite being connected with qualities that are causes of action. But what, then, is the quality in space that is a cause of action?
It is conjunction with air, dependent upon a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), just like the conjunction between air and a tree.

The answer to these two [objections] is stated in Nyāyasūtra 5.1.10: "Just as there is the cessation of the application of the material cause for a lamp, so too is there the cessation of that [application]."
First, when asked this, he ought to say: "Who takes up a lamp, and for what purpose? [The answer would be:
"Those desiring to see take it up for the purpose of seeing the object to be seen. Now, why do those desiring to see the lamp not take up another lamp?
If a lamp is seen even without reaching the end of another lamp, then the employment of a second lamp for the purpose of seeing that first lamp is useless.
Now, if it is asked for what purpose an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is stated, [the answer is]: "For the purpose of making known what is not yet understood.
Furthermore, for what purpose is the statement of the reason (*kāraṇāpadeśa*) sought in the case of an example?

If the example is cited for the purpose of making something known, then since an example is defined as "that object upon which there is a consensus of understanding among worldly investigators," the citation of a reason for the sake of making that known is useless; this is the response from the perspective of *prasaṅgasama* (balancing by consequence).
Alternatively, it is the response from the perspective of *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (balancing by a counter-example).
And when the counter-example functions as a reason, the example itself is not a non-reason.

By one who states a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), no specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*) is pointed out, in the sense that by this method the counter-example is the prover and not the [original] example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Thus, if the counter-example functions as the reason, it follows that the example is not a reason.
And how could that [counter-example] not be a reason?
If [the reason] were not refuted, it would be a prover.
NyS 5.1.12: The "balancing of non-arising" (anutpattisama) occurs because of the absence of a cause prior to the arising [of the effect].

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," another person says: "Prior to its production, while the sound has not yet arisen, the quality of following immediately upon effort—which is the cause of impermanence—is absent; therefore, by the absence of that [cause], it follows that it is permanent, and for that which is permanent, there is no production."
Objection based on non-arising is "balancing the non-arising" (anutpattisama).
The answer to this is: "Because that which has arisen exists in such a manner, and because the cause is established, there is no negation of the cause. (NyS 5.1.13)
"Because it exists as such once produced":
indeed, this sound comes to be as "produced";
prior to its production, the sound simply does not exist.

Since sound exists as something that has arisen, it is logical that its being produced immediately after effort is the cause of its impermanence; because such a cause is established, this objection—that "prior to its production there is an absence of a cause"—is untenable.

NyS 5.1.14: When the general property and the example are equally perceptible by the senses, [the fallacy] "balancing the doubt" (saṃśayasama) occurs because of the commonality of both permanence and impermanence.
When the reason has been stated— "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar"— an opponent objects by means of doubt:
"Even though it follows immediately upon effort, it possesses a common property (*sādharmya*) with the eternal *sāmānya*, namely its being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*),
and it also possesses it with the impermanent jar."
Therefore, because of the commonality of being both permanent and impermanent, doubt does not cease.
The answer to this is:

"If there is no doubt due to similarity when there is doubt, then there would be no doubt due to dissimilarity; or, if there were doubt in both cases, it would lead to an infinite regress of doubt. Furthermore, since permanence is not admitted, there is no refutation of the universal.
When the object is determined to be a 'person' based on a specific dissimilarity," (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.15).
Doubt does not find an opportunity based on the similarity between a post and a person;

likewise, when the impermanence of sound is ascertained through its dissimilarity—the specific property of being produced immediately after an effort—doubt does not find an opportunity based on the similarity between the permanent and the impermanent. If it were indeed to find such an opportunity, [it would be untenable].

Consequently, because the similarity between a post and a person would never cease, there would be perpetual doubt. Furthermore, when a distinguishing feature is perceived, it is not accepted that similarity remains a cause for doubt;
for once the specific characteristics of a person are perceived, the similarity between a post and a person does not serve as a cause for doubt.
The "neutralized" (prakaraṇasama) [reason] is that which establishes the subject matter through the commonality of both [sides].
NySBh_5,1.16: The process (*prakriyā*) is the engagement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) due to similarity with both the eternal and the non-eternal.
One person advances the thesis: "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately after effort, like a jar.
The second person advances the counter-thesis based on similarity with the eternal: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*)."

This being the case, when the reason "because it follows immediately upon effort" is stated by way of similarity with the impermanent, it does not transcend the context; and because it does not transcend the context, it does not transcend the lack of a definitive conclusion.
This is the same even when the reason is stated by way of similarity with the permanent.
This counter-position, which does not go beyond the original context, is *prakaraṇasama* (the "equivalent to the context").
This is the same even in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), because the process of proof is established through the dissimilarity to both; thus it is called *prakaraṇasama*.
Because the subject matter is established by means of a counter-argument, the negation is untenable, since the counter-argument itself is logically possible.
NySBh_5,1.17: By one who asserts that the establishment of a process results from similarity to both [sides], the establishment of a process through a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) has been stated.
If there is similarity to both, then one of them is a counter-position; this being the case, the counter-position becomes logically established.
The refutation is untenable because of the establishment of the counter-position;
if the establishment of the counter-position occurs, the refutation does not occur,
and if the establishment of the refutation occurs, the counter-position does not occur.
"It is a contradiction to claim both the establishment of a counter-position and the establishment of a refutation.
Furthermore, the completion of a formal inquiry (*prakriyā*) occurs through the determination of reality, because the inquiry concludes when the opposite [of uncertainty] is reached;
for it is only upon the determination of reality that the inquiry comes to an end.
The "equal to the non-reason" (ahetusama) occurs because the reason is not established in the three periods of time.

The reason (*hetu*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*); it must exist either prior to, after, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). If the means of proof exists prior [to the object to be proven],...
If the probandum does not exist, of what is there a proof?
Or if it exists later,
when the proof does not yet exist, of what is this the probandum?

Now, if the proof and the thing to be proven occur simultaneously, then since both exist at once, what is the proof of what, and what is the thing to be proven of what? Thus, the reason is not distinguished from a non-reason; because of its similarity to a non-reason, this is the "balancing of the non-reason" (ahetusama).
Since the probandum is established through the reason, there is no non-establishment [of the reason] across the three times.
There is no non-establishment [of the means] across the three times.
Why? Because the establishment of the probandum is from the probans.
The accomplishment of that which is to be accomplished and the cognition of that which is to be known—both are observed to arise from a cause.
Thus, this great object of direct perception serves as the illustrative example.
As for what was said— that if the probandum does not exist, of what is there a proof?—
it is of that which is produced and that which is made known.
And because the negation itself is untenable, there is no negation of that which is to be negated.
Whether the negation occurs before, after, or simultaneously, it is not tenable;
because such a negation is untenable, the probans for the establishment [of the thesis] is established.
Arthāpattisama (the equal by implication) occurs when the opponent's position is established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

NySBh_5.1.21: When the thesis has been established that "sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the *arthāpattisama* (balancing by implication) occurs for one who establishes a counter-thesis through implication (*arthāpatti*).

If, on the grounds of its similarity to the non-eternal due to following immediately upon effort, sound is non-eternal, it follows by implication that it must be eternal due to its similarity to the eternal.
And it possesses a commonality with that which is eternal, namely, the quality of being intangible.
The response to this is given in Nyāyasūtra 5.1.22:

"The occurrence of the loss of one's position through implication (*arthāpatti*) of what has not been stated is not established, because that which has not been stated is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and because implication itself is uncertain."

For one who asserts that "even without explicitly stating the capacity [of the reason], it follows by implication," there is the possibility of the loss of one's own position because [the loss] has not been explicitly stated;
for when the non-eternal position is established, the loss of the eternal position follows by implication. Furthermore, such an implication is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
This presumption (arthāpatti) is equal for both sides:
if sound is eternal because it possesses the common property of being intangible like space, then by implication, [the following must also hold].

"Because of the common property of impermanence, and because of being produced immediately after effort, [sound] is impermanent. Nor does this constitute an absolute presumption (*arthāpatti*) based merely on the opposite; for indeed, from the fact that a stone falls, it does not follow by implication that there is an absence of falling for liquid waters.

Nyāyasūtra 5.1.23: "The 'balancing of non-distinction' (*aviśeṣasama*) [occurs] because, if there is no distinction due to the occurrence of a single property, it would follow that everything is non-distinct, since existence occurs [in all things]."
NySBh_5,1.23: Since the single property of being produced immediately after an effort applies to both sound and a jar, there is no distinction between the two regarding their impermanence;
consequently, the consequence of total non-distinction follows.
How so? Because [the property] is established as existing [in both].
The counter-argument that "one property, namely existence, applies to everything;
for if existence were established, it would follow that all things are indistinguishable" is the *aviśeṣasama* (balancing the non-distinction).
In some cases there is the occurrence of that property, and in others its non-occurrence; therefore, there is no negation [of the reason].

Just as, because the single property of being produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is established for both the subject (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the other property of impermanence (*anityatva*) constitutes a non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*);
it is not so with all existing things (*sarvabhāva*), for there is no other property that serves as the cause for the establishment of their existence by which a non-distinction could occur.

Now, if it is thought that impermanence itself would be another property (*dharmāntara*) serving as the cause for the existence of entities everywhere, then, when conceived in this way, the thesis (*pakṣa*) follows: "All entities are impermanent because they possess existence.
In that case, there is no example other than the very meaning of the proposition itself.
Furthermore, there is no example for the reason, "it does not exist";
moreover, it is untenable for a part of the thesis itself to serve as the example,
for that which is to be proven cannot be the example.
Furthermore, because existence possesses both permanence and impermanence, impermanence is not established.
Therefore, since the establishment of existence leads to the consequence that all things would be indistinguishable, this statement is devoid of meaning.
By asserting that all things are impermanent because their existence is established, you have admitted the impermanence of sound.
In that case, the negation is untenable.
NyS 5.1.25: The "equal to the proof" (upapattisama) [fallacy] occurs because the reasons for both [the thesis and its opposite] are equally applicable.

NySBh_5,1.25: If a cause for the non-eternality of sound is established, then sound is non-eternal; yet a cause for its eternality, namely its intangibility (*asparśatva*), is also established, and thus eternality is likewise established.
To counter-argue by establishing the causes for both non-eternality and eternality is the "balancing by proof" (*upapattisama*).
NS 5.1.26: There is no refutation [of the opponent's position] because you have admitted the reason for its establishment.
By stating "because both types of causes are applicable," it is not denied that impermanence exists because the cause of impermanence is applicable;
for if it were denied, there would be no applicability of both types of causes.
By the statement "because both types of causes are applicable," the applicability of the cause of impermanence is admitted.
The prohibition is untenable because it has been granted permission. If you argue that the prohibition is valid due to contradiction, then the contradiction is equal [in both cases].
If it is argued that by stating a contradiction— namely, the consequence that a single entity would be both eternal and non-eternal— one has provided a refutation,
then the contradiction is equal for both one's own position and the opponent's; and since it is equal, it cannot establish either one.
The "balancing by perception" (upalabdhisama) occurs because [the probandum] is perceived even in the absence of the stated cause.

NySBh_5.1.27: Even in the absence of the stated cause of impermanence—namely, being produced immediately after an effort—the impermanence of sound arising from the snapping of a tree branch due to the impact of wind is observed.
To raise an objection based on the observation of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) even in the absence of the stated probans (*sādhana*) is the "balancing by perception" (*upalabdhisama*).
The answer to this is:
"There is no refutation, because that property can also arise from another cause" (NyS 5.1.28).
By stating "because it follows immediately after effort," the production [of sound] from a cause is being expressed,
not a restriction of the effect to that specific cause.
And if the impermanence of sound is established even when it is produced from another cause, [then the argument holds].
What is it that is being negated here?
It is not the case that a sound which already exists is unperceived prior to its utterance; why?
Because no such thing as a veil (āvaraṇa) or similar obstacle is perceived.

Just as there is non-perception of an existing object like water due to the presence of a veil or the like, it is not so with sound, for its non-perception does not result from a cause of non-apprehension such as a veil.
This [non-apprehension] would be apprehended as the cause for its non-apprehension, just like water and so forth; yet it is not apprehended.
Therefore, sound is the opposite of water and such things insofar as it is not perceived.

(NyS 5.1.29) Since its non-existence is established by the non-perception of that [non-apprehension], and because the opposite of that [non-existence] is thus possible, this is the "balancing of non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhisama*).
The non-perception of those [factors] such as obstruction is not itself perceived.

Because it is not perceived, its non-existence is established by the principle that "what is not perceived does not exist. Since there is no cause for establishing its non-existence, the opposite—namely, the existence of obstruction and the rest—is determined.
Because the opposite of that is established, the thesis previously asserted—that "there is no non-perception of an existing sound prior to its utterance"—is not proven.

Thus, this reason—"because of the non-perception of an obstruction and so forth"—is countered by the non-perception of the obstruction itself (and other such factors) through the non-perception of the convention; this constitutes the *anupalabdhisama* (the equalization based on non-perception).
The reply to this is: "Because non-apprehension has the nature of non-apprehension, it is not a valid reason. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.30)
The non-perception of an obstruction and so forth is not [a proof that] it does not exist, because it is itself non-perception; thus, it is not a valid reason.
Why? Because non-perception has the nature of non-perception.
Because non-apprehension is merely the absence of apprehension;
that which exists is the object of apprehension,
and it is asserted that "it exists" by means of apprehension.
That which does not exist is the object of non-apprehension;
it is asserted that what is not apprehended does not exist.

This non-apprehension, which arises from the non-apprehension of an obscuration and so forth, operates within its own domain when there is an absence of apprehension—that is, when there is no apprehension—and it does not negate its own domain.
And non-prohibition [of perception] is fit to serve as the reason for the non-perception of an obstruction and so forth; however,
since obstructions and the like exist, they are objects of perception,
and therefore their perception ought to occur.

Since those [obstacles] are not perceived—that is, because there is an absence of a perception that establishes its own object—it is understood through non-perception that the object of non-perception is as follows: "there are no causes for the non-apprehension of sound, such as obstructions.
For it is through non-perception that non-perception itself is established.
That object belongs to it.
And because one internally experiences the presence and absence of conceptual cognitions.
The term "non-reason" (ahetu) carries over from the previous context.
In each individual body, the existence and non-existence of various cognitions are to be experienced through direct awareness, such as:
"I have a cognition of doubt," or "I do not have a cognition of doubt."
The same applies to the cognitions of perception, inference, scripture, and memory.

This non-perception of an obstruction and so forth is the absence of perception; it is self-cognized in the form: "I have no perception of an obstruction or the like of the sound. Thus, one does not perceive the causes for the non-apprehension of the sound, such as obstructions.
In this regard, that which was stated—that the establishment of non-existence follows from the non-perception of that [non-perception]—is [thus explained].
This is not tenable.

The "balancing of the non-eternal" (anityasama) occurs when, because of similarity—that is, the occurrence of a common property—there follows the undesirable consequence that everything must be non-eternal.

The "balancing by non-eternality" (anityasama) occurs because, due to similarity—that is, the occurrence of a common property—there follows the undesirable consequence that everything would be non-eternal.

5.1.32: For one who says, "Sound is impermanent because of its similarity to an impermanent jar," since there is a similarity between the impermanent jar and all entities, it follows that the impermanence of all things results—which is undesirable.
This is the "balancing the impermanent" (*anityasama*), so called because it is an opposition based on impermanence.
Here is the reply to this:
Because it is unestablished due to similarity, the negation is unestablished, owing to its similarity with that which is to be negated.

NySBh_5,1.33: A statement consisting of the members [of a syllogism] beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) which subverts the position and is characterized as a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) is a refutation (*pratiṣedha*).
Its similarity (*sādharmya*) with the position—that which is to be refuted—consists in its connection with the proposition and the other members.
If, on account of this similarity with the impermanent, the non-eternality [of sound] were not established, [then the same would apply to the case of the eternal].
Because it shares the same properties [as the unestablished], the negation is also unestablished; for it shares the same properties with that which is to be negated.

And since, in the example, the property known through the relationship of the probandum and the probans serves as the reason, and because that [property] exists in both ways, there is no lack of distinction.
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), that property which is indeed known through the relationship of the probandum and the probans is stated as the reason (*hetu*).
And that [reason] exists in two ways.
It is similar to something in some respects and distinguished from it in others;
from the similarity comes the commonality (*sādharmya*), and from the distinction comes the difference (*vaidharmya*). Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is a specific instance of commonality.
It is not the case that mere similarity or mere dissimilarity without qualification [constitutes a fallacy].

By relying on mere similarity and mere dissimilarity, you have said: "Because of similarity, due to the occurrence of a common property, there follows the undesirable consequence of the non-eternality of all things; this is 'the equalization by non-eternality' (anityasama).
This is incorrect.
And that which was stated regarding the refutation of the "equivalence through non-distinction" (aviśeṣasama) should also be understood here.
The "balancing of the eternal" (nityasama) occurs because, since the eternal is observed to have an impermanent state, it follows that permanence is established even in the impermanent.
It is proposed that sound is impermanent.
Is that impermanence permanent in sound or impermanent? If it exists at all times, [then sound would be permanent].
Because the property (dharma) exists at all times, the substratum (dharmī) must also exist at all times; thus, sound is eternal.
Or, if it does not exist at all times, then because the property of impermanence is absent, sound is eternal.
Thus, because it is countered on the grounds of permanence, it is the "balancing of permanence" (nityasama).
The answer to this is:
Since the permanent is always absent from that which is to be negated, and since non-permanence is established only in the impermanent, there is no negation [of permanence].
When it is stated that "because non-eternality always exists in the sound which is the object of negation," the non-eternality of sound is admitted;
and since non-eternality is thus established, the negation "sound is not non-eternal" is untenable.
If, on the other hand, this is not accepted, [the reason remains unestablished].
"Because non-eternality exists eternally, [the reason] is not a valid reason; thus, due to the absence of a reason, the negation is untenable.
Or rather, the non-existence of sound due to the cessation of what has arisen is its non-eternality; in that case, the counter-question is untenable.
This inquiry—whether this impermanence exists at all times in sound or not—is untenable.
Why? Because impermanence is the non-existence of sound due to the cessation of that which has arisen.
This being the case, there is no distinction between the locus and the located due to contradiction;
furthermore, because of the opposition between permanence and impermanence,
permanence and impermanence as two attributes of a single substratum (dharmin) are mutually exclusive.
This is not possible.
In that regard, what was stated— that "because impermanence exists in the permanent, it must be permanent itself"— was said with reference to something that does not actually exist.
NyS 5.1.37: [The fallacy] called "balancing the effect" (kāryasama) occurs because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort.
"Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort.
That which acquires its own existence immediately after effort indeed comes into being after not having existed,
just like an effect such as a jar.
It is understood that "impermanent" means having come into being, it no longer exists.
This being the case, the refutation is stated on the grounds that "the effects of effort are manifold.
Furthermore, the acquisition of their own nature immediately following effort is observed in the case of jars and other such things.
Furthermore, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) consists in the removal of obstructions for things that are concealed;
thus, there is no distinction as to whether the sound acquires its own nature immediately after effort or whether it is manifested.
To object on the basis of the non-distinction of the effect is the "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*) sophistry.
The answer to this is:
"If there were a difference in the effect, effort would not be the cause, because the conditions for non-perception are present. (NyS 5.1.38)

If there were a difference between the effect [of production] and [the effect of] manifestation, then effort would not be the cause for the manifestation of sound, because the causes of non-perception would be applicable.

Where manifestation occurs immediately after effort, an obstruction as a cause of non-perception is applicable; and through the removal of that obstruction, there occurs the manifestation characterized by the perception of the object that exists immediately after the effort.
However, no cause for the non-perception of sound is established, such that the manifestation characterized by perception would occur upon the removal of that [cause] immediately after effort;
therefore, sound is produced, it is not manifested.
If the reason is established as being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), then because of its inconclusiveness, it would be non-probative;
and if non-probativeness follows from inconclusiveness, then the same fault applies equally to the refutation as well. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.39)
The negation is also inconclusive; because it negates some things while not negating others, it is inconclusive and therefore not a proof.
Alternatively, on the position that sound is non-eternal, there is no specific reason [to distinguish] that what occurs immediately after effort is its production and not its manifestation.
Even on the view that [sound] is eternal, there is no specific reason [to prefer one side], as the manifestation occurs immediately after effort rather than its production;
thus, this absence of a specific reason applies equally to both positions, and consequently, both are inconclusive.
In all cases, it is thus.

NySBh_5,1.40: In all the reasons for refutation beginning with "similarity" (*sādharmya*), wherever a lack of distinction is observed, it follows that [the fallacy] applies equally to both sides of the argument.
In the counter-refutation of a refutation, there is a fault similar to the fault in the original refutation.
This same inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) which constitutes an equal defect even in the case of the negation, remains equally applicable when there is a counter-negation of that negation.
In this regard, the first position is the proponent’s formal argument: "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately after effort.

The second position is the opponent’s counter-argument, which serves as a refutation by means of a reason for negation: "Because there is a plurality of effects produced by effort, [the reason] is equivalent to the effect (*kāryasama*)."
And that [original argument] is called a "prohibition" (pratiṣedha).
Since the same fault applies even to this prohibition, the third position is called a "counter-prohibition" (vipratiṣedha).
Since the same fault and the lack of certainty (anaikāntikatva) apply even to this counter-prohibition, the fourth position is established.
Having admitted that the refutation is faulty, to apply an identical consequence of fault to the counter-refutation is "admission of the opponent's position" (matānujñā).

The fifth position is as follows: having accepted the second position—the negation—as being faulty, and without having refuted it, the proponent of the refutation (dūṣaṇavādī) incurs the fault of "accepting the opponent's view" (matānujñā) by applying the same counter-argument that the non-conclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) is equal in the third position, which is the negation of the negation (pratiṣedhavipratiṣedha). Thus, the charge of matānujñā follows.

NyS 5.1.43: When a reason is stated in the conclusion of an argument supported by proof that depends on the characteristics of one's own position, the fault is the same because one has admitted the fault of the opponent's position.

In the case of the establishing position (*sthāpanā*), the fault that "because there is a multiplicity of effects of effort" belongs to the proponent of the establishing reason as a characteristic of his own position. Why? Because it originates from his own position.

Thus, while overlooking this fault characterized by his own position and failing to extract it, he—having admitted it—attributes the same fault to the opposing position by stating, "the fault is equal even in the refutation," thereby applying a fault that is established [for himself] to the other's position.

Thus, he points out the reason that the negation is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). In that case, when there is both the attribution of a fault that is applicable with respect to the definition of one's own position (*svapakṣa*) and the statement of a reason, the fault of the opponent’s position (*parapakṣa*) becomes accepted by him. How so?

Without having removed the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) that was stated by the opponent through the argument beginning with "because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort," he says that the same fault applies to the refutation as well.
Thus, for one who, having accepted that the proof (sthāpanā) is faulty, then attributes the same fault to the refutation, the fault becomes equal because of his acceptance of the opponent's position.

Just as it was argued that by accepting the opponent's refutation as faulty, one incurs the same fault even when offering a counter-refutation, and thus the consequence of "admission of the opponent's position" (matānujñā) follows;
so too, by accepting the proponent's original thesis as faulty and then attributing the same fault to its refutation, the consequence of "admission of the opponent's position" follows.
This indeed constitutes the sixth position.

In this regard, the first, third, and fifth positions belong to those who argue by means of a probans for establishment (*sthāpanāhetuvādin*), while the second, fourth, and sixth positions belong to those who argue by means of a probans for negation (*pratiṣedhahetuvādin*). When their validity or invalidity is being examined, since there is no difference in meaning between the fourth and sixth positions, they fall into the fault of tautology (*punarukta*).
Furthermore, regarding the fourth position, it is stated that the opponent incurs the same fault: "In the negation of a negation, the fault is the same as the fault in the negation."

In the sixth [case] as well, it is stated that "the fault is the same because one accepts the fault in the opponent's position," which refers only to the equality of the fault; there is no specific difference in meaning.
Furthermore, the consequence of the fault of redundancy is the same for the third and fifth cases.
In the third position as well, equality is accepted on the grounds that "the same fault applies even in the negation.
In the fifth position too, it is accepted that "in the counter-negation of the negation, the same fault follows," such that no specific distinction in meaning is stated.
In that regard, because there is no difference in meaning between the fifth and sixth positions, they incur the fault of tautology;
between the third and fourth, there is the concession of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*);
and between the first and second, there is an absence of a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*). Thus, in this "six-position" argument (*ṣaṭpakṣī*), neither side achieves proof.
When is there a "sixfold cycle" (*ṣaṭpakṣī*)?
When [the argument] proceeds thus: "Even in the case of a negation, the fault is the same. Then, neither of the two positions is established.
But when the third position is refuted by the statement, "If there were a difference in the effect, effort would not be the cause, because the causes for non-perception are present," then—

by virtue of stating a specific reason that "the sound acquires its own nature immediately after effort, rather than being manifested"— the first position is established, and thus the sixfold dialectical cycle (*ṣaṭpakṣī*) does not proceed.
